summary: The note examines recent initiatives in Seattle, Atlanta and New York City that bring marginalized communities into urban development planning. It outlines the principles behind effective engagement (accessibility, safety and trust, transparency, accountability), reported outcomes, and persistent challenges such as bureaucratic inertia, funding limits and hard-to-reach groups. It concludes that cities should institutionalize these practices to build more resilient, equitable cities.
one_line: Recent city programs in Seattle, Atlanta and New York engage marginalized communities in urban planning, with notable outcomes and ongoing challenges.
key_facts: Since September 1, 2023, the note says there has been a marked shift toward greater inclusivity in urban planning.
The "City for All" program was launched in October 2023 in Seattle, Washington, spearheaded by City Councilor Maria Gonzalez to bring low-income residents and people of color into urban planning.
"City for All" relies on community workshops and forums, plus an online platform to collect input from people unable to attend in person.
Participants in "City for All" sessions asked for more affordable housing, accessible transport, and green spaces in their neighborhoods.
Urban planner James Lee started the "Voices at the Margins" campaign in Atlanta, Georgia in January 2024 to include LGBTQ+ individuals' insights in the city's restructuring plans.
"Voices at the Margins" uses cultural events such as art installations and poetry readings while surveying participants about their urban life experiences.
New York City's initiative, led by Deputy Mayor Anita Richardson and launched in February 2024, focuses on the homeless population and employs former homeless individuals as liaisons.
Four core principles of effective engagement are accessibility, safety and trust, transparency, and accountability.
Seattle's "City for All" led to a new affordable housing project with community-suggested design elements such as community gardens and child-friendly spaces.
After "Voices at the Margins", Atlanta planners added more well-lit pedestrian zones and created safer public restrooms to be more inclusive for the LGBTQ+ community.

Challenges include bureaucratic inertia, resistance from established power structures, financial constraints causing partial incorporation of suggestions, and hard-to-reach groups like the transient homeless.
The note says cities should institutionalize engagement practices, which requires strong political will and resources, and that inclusion can make cities more resilient and sustainable.
